concepts.name: First Amendment (1951): Addition of Article 31A and 31B
key_dimensions: Why 1st Amendment was necessitated — judicial invalidation of zamindari abolition laws in State of Bihar v. Kameshwar Singh (1952)
Article 31A: Protection of laws relating to acquisition of estates from Articles 14 and 19 — scope and limitations
Article 31B: Ninth Schedule shield — original intent vs. post-IR Coelho (2007) judicial review applicability
UPSC trap: 1st Amendment added 31A and 31B but did NOT alter the text of any existing DPSP article

concepts.name: Fourth Amendment (1955): Expansion of Article 31A and Ninth Schedule
key_dimensions: Extended the categories of laws protected under Article 31A beyond just 'estates' to include management of properties, amalgamation of corporations, extinguishment of rights
Added more zamindari abolition laws to the Ninth Schedule
Relationship to DPSP Article 39(b) and (c) — equitable distribution of material resources
UPSC trap: Distinguish between 1st Amendment and 4th Amendment expansions of 31A scope

concepts.name: Twenty-Fifth Amendment (1971): Insertion of Article 31C
key_dimensions: Article 31C: Laws giving effect to Article 39(b) and (c) cannot be challenged on grounds of violating Articles 14, 19 — original scope limited to two DPSPs
Second part of 31C (making such laws non-justiciable) struck down in Kesavananda Bharati (1973)
Minerva Mills (1980): Confirmed that only 39(b) and (c) are protected, not all DPSPs — Supreme Court struck down expansion made by 42nd Amendment
UPSC trap: 25th Amendment added 31C; 42nd Amendment tried to expand it to ALL DPSPs — that expansion was invalidated

concepts.name: Forty-Second Amendment (1976): DPSP vs. Fundamental Rights — Supremacy Clause
key_dimensions: Added Articles 48A (environment) and 43A (workers' participation in industry) as new DPSPs
Attempted to give DPSPs supremacy over Fundamental Rights under Articles 14, 19, and 31 — declared unconstitutional in Minerva Mills (1980)
Expanded Article 31C protection to ALL DPSPs — struck down by Supreme Court
UPSC trap: 42nd Amendment is simultaneously the most pro-DPSP amendment AND the most judicially reversed amendment

concepts.name: Article 48A (Environment Protection) — Inserted by 42nd Amendment
key_dimensions: Directs the State to protect and improve the environment and safeguard forests and wildlife — inserted as a DPSP, not a Fundamental Right
Read alongside Article 51A(g) — Fundamental Duty to protect environment — creating a complementary pair
Judicial elevation: Courts have used 48A to derive the right to a clean environment under Article 21 (Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar, 1991)
UPSC trap: 48A is a DPSP (Part IV), while 51A(g) is a Fundamental Duty (Part IVA) — both added by 42nd Amendment but in different Parts

concepts.name: Article 43A (Workers' Participation in Management) — Inserted by 42nd Amendment
key_dimensions: Directs the State to secure participation of workers in the management of undertakings
Legislative implementation: Companies Act provisions on worker directors in public sector undertakings
Relationship with Article 43 (living wage) — both deal with labour welfare but at different levels
UPSC trap: Article 43A is not about minimum wages (that is Article 43) — common confusion in Prelims

concepts.name: Forty-Fourth Amendment (1978): Deletion of Article 31 (Right to Property) and Article 19(1)(f)
key_dimensions: Deleted Article 19(1)(f) (right to acquire/hold/dispose property) and Article 31 (right to property) from Fundamental Rights
Inserted Article 300A — right to property as a constitutional right (not fundamental right) in Part XII
Impact on DPSP-FR conflict: Removed the primary basis of conflict between Article 39(b)(c) and property rights
UPSC trap: Right to property is still a constitutional/legal right under 300A but can be restricted without the strict scrutiny applicable to Fundamental Rights

concepts.name: Eighty-Sixth Amendment (2002): Article 21A and Corresponding DPSP Change
key_dimensions: Added Article 21A — Right to Education as a Fundamental Right for children 6–14 years

Amended Article 45 (DPSP) — original Article 45 directed free and compulsory education for children up to 14 years; post-86th Amendment it was changed to early childhood care for children below 6 years
This is a rare case where a DPSP was AMENDED (not just added) and its content was partially 'upgraded' to a Fundamental Right
UPSC trap: Post-86th Amendment, Article 45 now covers ONLY children BELOW 6 years; children 6–14 are covered by Article 21A as a Fundamental Right

concepts.name: Ninety-Seventh Amendment (2011): Cooperative Societies and DPSPs
key_dimensions: Inserted Article 43B as a new DPSP — promotion of cooperative societies
Also inserted Article 19(1)(c) amendment to include right to form cooperative societies as a Fundamental Right

Partially struck down in Rajendra N. Shah v. Union of India (2021) — Part relating to state cooperative societies struck down as it invaded states' domain without ratification by states under Article 368(2)
UPSC trap: 97th Amendment added BOTH a Fundamental Right (19(1)(c) expansion) AND a DPSP (43B) simultaneously — and was partially invalidated

concepts.name: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973): Basic Structure and DPSPs
key_dimensions: Struck down the second part of Article 31C that made DPSP-implementing laws non-justiciable
Established that Fundamental Rights are part of Basic Structure — Parliament cannot destroy them even to implement DPSPs
However, upheld the first part of 31C — laws implementing 39(b) and (c) are protected from 14 and 19 challenge
UPSC trap: Kesavananda did NOT make DPSPs unimportant — it struck a BALANCE, not a hierarchy favoring only FRs

concepts.name: Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980): Harmonious Construction Doctrine
key_dimensions: Struck down Section 4 of 42nd Amendment that expanded 31C to ALL DPSPs — held it violated Basic Structure
Established the doctrine: Balance between Fundamental Rights and DPSPs is part of Basic Structure
Reaffirmed that Article 31C protection is limited only to Articles 39(b) and (c)
UPSC trap: Minerva Mills is the case that set the CEILING on DPSP supremacy — Parliament cannot give DPSPs blanket supremacy over ALL Fundamental Rights

concepts.name: I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007): Ninth Schedule Judicial Review
key_dimensions: Nine-judge bench held: Laws added to Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973 (date of Kesavananda judgment) CAN be judicially reviewed if they violate Basic Structure
Effectively limited the absolute immunity of the Ninth Schedule for post-1973 insertions
Direct impact on 31B: Laws in Ninth Schedule that violate Fundamental Rights forming part of Basic Structure (like Articles 14, 15, 21) are no longer absolutely immune
UPSC trap: Pre-April 24, 1973 Ninth Schedule laws still have absolute immunity; only POST-1973 insertions are subject to Basic Structure review

concepts.name: State of Kerala v. N.M. Thomas (1976): Article 16(4) and DPSP Relationship
key_dimensions: Held that reservations under Article 16(4) are not an exception to Article 16(1) but a facet of it — enabling DPSPs on social justice to be implemented without conflict
Connected DPSP Article 46 (promotion of educational and economic interests of SCs/STs) with Fundamental Right Article 16
Demonstrated judicial technique of reading DPSPs and FRs harmoniously rather than as conflicting
UPSC trap: This case pre-dates Mandal Commission but establishes key principle that DPSPs can INFORM the interpretation of Fundamental Rights

concepts.name: Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981): Ninth Schedule and Post-Kesavananda Laws
key_dimensions: Confirmed the April 24, 1973 cut-off for Ninth Schedule immunity established in IR Coelho
Laws placed in Ninth Schedule before Kesavananda judgment are valid and cannot be challenged
This case is important for understanding the CHRONOLOGICAL dimension of Ninth Schedule protection
UPSC trap: Waman Rao (1981) and IR Coelho (2007) both deal with Ninth Schedule review but Waman Rao deals with pre-1973 laws while IR Coelho addresses post-1973 laws

concepts.name: Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985): DPSPs and Article 21 Expansion
key_dimensions: Held that DPSP Article 39(a) (right to adequate means of livelihood) can be read into Article 21 to include 'right to livelihood'
Demonstrated the judicial technique of using DPSPs to EXPAND the content of Fundamental Rights
Pavement dwellers case — eviction without alternative arrangements violated expanded Article 21
UPSC trap: DPSPs are non-justiciable by themselves but become enforceable when courts READ them INTO Fundamental Rights — this is the key judicial innovation

concepts.name: Unnikrishnan v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1993): Right to Education Pre-86th Amendment
key_dimensions: Before 86th Amendment, Supreme Court derived right to education for children up to 14 years from Article 21 read with Article 45 (DPSP)
Showed how a DPSP (45) provided the substantive content to a Fundamental Right (21)
After 86th Amendment (2002), this judicial derivation was replaced by explicit Article 21A — but the case demonstrates DPSP's role in expanding FRs
UPSC trap: Right to education existed as a Fundamental Right JUDICIALLY (post-1993 via Art. 21+45) before it was made explicit by 86th Amendment (2002)

concepts.name: Forty-Second Amendment (1976): New DPSPs — Articles 39A, 43A, 48A
key_dimensions: Article 39A: Equal justice and free legal aid — basis for Legal Services Authorities Act 1987 and NALSA
Article 43A: Workers' participation in management of industries
Article 48A: Protection of environment, forests, and wildlife
UPSC trap: 42nd Amendment added THREE new DPSPs (39A, 43A, 48A) — the most DPSPs added by any single amendment; also simultaneously attempted (unsuccessfully) to give all DPSPs supremacy over FRs

concepts.name: Article 39(b) and (c): Material Resources Distribution — Constitutional Interpretation
key_dimensions: Article 39(b): Distribution of ownership and control of material resources for common good; Article 39(c): Prevention of concentration of wealth
These are the ONLY two DPSPs that enjoy special protection under Article 31C (post-Minerva Mills)

Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra (2024): Nine-judge bench reconsidered whether 'material resources' includes privately owned resources — partially overruled State of Karnataka v. Ranganatha Reddy (1977)
UPSC trap: Among ALL DPSPs, only 39(b) and (c) have constitutional backing to override Articles 14 and 19 — this is unique to them alone

concepts.name: Distinction between Amendability of DPSPs vs. Fundamental Rights
key_dimensions: DPSPs can be amended by simple majority in Parliament in terms of procedural requirements under Article 368 — but substantive limits apply via Basic Structure doctrine
Fundamental Rights amendments require 2/3rd majority + majority of total membership; some also require state ratification
42nd Amendment tried to make DPSPs override FRs — Minerva Mills held the BALANCE between the two is itself Basic Structure and cannot be disturbed

UPSC trap: There is NO provision in the Constitution that explicitly states DPSPs are subordinate to FRs — this hierarchy is ENTIRELY judge-made through Champakam Dorairajan (1951) and subsequent cases

concepts.name: Champakam Dorairajan v. State of Madras (1951): First DPSP vs. FR Conflict
key_dimensions: First case where Supreme Court held that Fundamental Rights prevail over DPSPs in case of conflict — state communal reservation in education violated Article 29(2)
This judgment directly TRIGGERED the First Amendment (1951) — Parliament added Article 15(4) to override this judgment
Established the original (pre-42nd Amendment) doctrine: In case of conflict, FRs prevail over DPSPs

UPSC trap: Champakam Dorairajan is the ONLY case that established FR supremacy over DPSPs and was immediately 'reversed' by a constitutional amendment (1st Amendment adding Art. 15(4)) — unique example of amendment overturning a Supreme Court judgment
